blocks.text: Turkmen cooking grew out of a life with flocks of sheep, and meat, bread and tea are at its heart. Three dishes show it well: *palaw* for celebrations and honoured guests, *dograma* for the great family occasions, and *gutap* for every day.

*Palaw*, the rice dish known across Central Asia as pilaf or plov, is defined in the Turkmen explanatory dictionary as a dish of rice cooked on meat fried in oil, with chopped onion and carrot and water poured over. The meat is usually mutton. It is made in a *gazan*, a large round iron cauldron set over an open fire, and served on one big dish in the middle of the cloth, where it is traditionally eaten with the right hand. A Turkmen proverb says you need more than talk to cook it:

blocks.tk: Gury sözden palaw bolmaz, ýag bilen tüwisi bolmasa.
blocks.en: Empty words won't make a palaw, without its oil and its rice.
blocks.source: Turkmen proverb, quoted in the explanatory dictionary under palaw

blocks.text: *Dograma* takes its name from *dogramak*, to cut or tear into pieces. Flatbread is baked, often in the clay oven, the tamdyr, you met in [A1 unit 8](a1-u08-culture), while mutton boils for hours in the gazan. Then the bread is torn by hand into small pieces, mixed with onion and the shredded meat, and served in bowls with the hot broth poured over. It is a dish for special days, such as the holiday of Gurbanlyk, when families, friends and neighbours visit each other.

Making dograma is a shared job. The bread is usually baked by the women of the house, and tearing it into small pieces is work for the whole family, sometimes the neighbours too, sitting together around a cloth.

*Gutap* is simpler: a thin circle of dough filled with minced meat, pumpkin or greens such as spinach, folded into a half-moon and cooked on a hot pan. It is sold at bazaars and roadside stalls and eaten on the go, and it is made at home too.

blocks.title: At the table
blocks.text: A host says *Buýruň!* (please, help yourself) and, to a guest, *Iýiň, içiň!* (eat, drink!). The guest answers *Sag boluň!* And to choose: *Palaw ýa-da dograma?*
With the words of this unit, you can read this:

blocks.tk: Myhmanlar gelýär. Ejäm: “Geliň, oturyň! Buýruň, palaw iýiň!” Kakam dograma üçin çörek getirýär. Men palaw isleýärin, emma jigim gutap isleýär.
blocks.en: The guests are arriving. My mother says: “Come in, sit down! Please, have some pilaf!” My father is bringing bread for the dograma. I want pilaf, but my younger brother wants gutap.

questions.q: What does the name *dograma* come from?

questions.explain: The clay oven is the *tamdyr*, and the cloth is the *saçak*.

questions.q: In the reading, what does the writer's younger brother want?
questions.explain: *emma jigim gutap isleýär*: but my younger brother wants gutap.

sources.title: Turkmen cuisine
sources.note: Palaw served at celebrations and to honoured guests, with mutton, carrots and onions; the gazan, a large hemispherical iron pot over an open fire; gutap often filled with spinach, sold at roadside stands

sources.title: Dograma
sources.note: The name from dogramak, to cut into pieces; reserved for special occasions such as Gurbanlyk; bread torn by the whole family; served with hot broth

sources.title: Turkmen Holiday Dishes
sources.note: Pilaf served on a large plate and traditionally eaten with the right hand; women bake the bread for dograma; family and sometimes neighbours help
